title: get_pvalue(... , direction = "both") returns incorrect value in some cases
description:
`get_pvalue(... , direction = "both")` appears to return an incorrect value when the sample test statistic is present in null hypothesis test statistic distribution. This is rarely observed when the number of permuted replicates is small, but when that number is large it happens. When this happens it is as if the code does this:

```
sum(abs(null_distribution$stat) > abs(delta_sample))/number_of_permutations 
```

when it should do this:
```
sum(abs(null_distribution$stat) >= abs(delta_sample))/number_of_permutations
```

The key difference between these being the  `>` vs `>=`. 

Here is some data and a minimum working example that replicates this:

#### data:
[click_through.csv.zip](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/files/2516748/click_through.csv.zip)

#### code:
```
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
click_through <- read_csv("click_through.csv")

delta_sample <- click_through %>% group_by(webpage) %>% 
  summarize(stat = mean(click_target)) %>% 
  summarize(stat = diff(stat)) %>% unlist()

set.seed(2018)
null_distribution <- click_through %>% 
  mutate(click_target = factor(click_target), webpage = factor(webpage)) %>% 
  specify(formula = click_target ~ webpage, success = "1")  %>% 
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% 
  generate(reps = 15000)  %>% 
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("Services", "Interact"))
```

If I calculate the p-value with `p_value` I get:

```{r}
null_distribution %>% 
  get_pvalue(obs_stat = delta_sample, direction = "both") %>% 
  unlist()
```

```
    p_value 
0.001066667 
```

Whereas, if I calculate the p-value "manually" I get:
 
```{r}
sum(abs(null_distribution$stat) >= abs(delta_sample))/number_of_permutations
```

```
[1] 0.0018
```

If I incorrectly calculate the  p-value "manually" using `>` instead of `>=` I get the same answer as that returned from `get_pvalue`:
```{r}
sum(abs(null_distribution$stat) > abs(delta_sample))/number_of_permutations
```

```
[1] 0.001066667
```

I tried to look at the source code of `get_pvalue` and can see that calls `get_percentile` which uses `stats::ecdf` to get the probabilities (instead of counting as I did). So I am naively guessing its something to do with wanting the value from `stats::ecdf` of the xi previous than the one that is currently getting returned (the lagged value)?

title: Extend `calculate()` with stat = "diff in weighted means"
description:
Currently `calculate()` offers with `stat= "diff in means"` an interface, which some situations does not provide enough control. 

In following example I want to see the Volume-weighted diff in means.

Can `calculate()` be extended to offer `stat= "diff in weighted means"` ?

```
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)

# Random data 
n= 25
set.seed(42)
data_example= tibble(Product= c(rep("A", n/2), rep("B", n/2)),
                    Price= c(rnorm(n= n/2, mean= 2, sd = 0.2), 
                             rnorm(n= (n/2)-5, mean= 3, sd = 0.3),
                             rnorm(n= 5, mean= 2.2, sd = 0.2)),
                    Volume= c(rnorm(n= n/2, mean= 100, sd = 5), 
                              rnorm(n= (n/2)-5, mean= 10, sd = 1),
                              rnorm(n= 5, mean= 100, sd = 5)))

summary(data_example)
# Visualize
# as you can see the Volume-weighted difference is pritty small between Product B and A.
ggplot(data_example) + geom_jitter(aes(x= factor(Product), y= Price, size= Volume), width = 0.1, alpha= 0.5)
ggplot(data_example) + geom_boxplot(aes(x= factor(Product), y= Price))


## Unweighted

# effect
(d_hat= data_example %>% 
    specify(Price ~ Product) %>%
    calculate(stat= "diff in means", order = c("B", "A"))
)

# h0
null_distn= data_example %>%
  specify(Price ~ Product) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("B", "A"))

# visualize
visualize(null_distn) +
  shade_p_value(obs_stat = d_hat, direction = "greater")

# p-value
# As this is calculated without considering the Volume-weights, the p-value is small and might be misleading in most situations.
null_distn %>% 
  get_p_value(obs_stat = d_hat, direction = "greater")



# Weighted 
# Testing with Volume-weights, the p-value is more appropriate.
library(weights)
a= data_example %>% filter(Product=="A")
b= data_example %>% filter(Product=="B")
wtd.t.test(x = b$Price, y = a$Price, weight = b$Volume, weighty = a$Volume, 
           alternative = "greater")
```

title: Showing p-values and confidence intervals automatically on charts created using Visualize()
description: IMO it would be a nice addition to show the p value and CI interval automatically as annotation on the plot created using the visualize function. Maybe adding a parameter to control this behavior (to display p value or not) along with another parameter to control the position (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) would be good. Default for this new parameter could be set to not display the p-value.

title: Syntax for the theoretical shortcut
description:
In the `develop` branch, this is the sort of syntax that we use to generate the theoretical chi-squared distribution in this case.
```
fli_small %>%
  specify(origin ~ season) %>% # alt: response = origin, explanatory = season
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  # calculate(stat = "Chisq") ## Not needed since Chisq is implied
  visualize(method = "theoretical", obs_stat = obs_chisq, direction = "right")
```
That is, the "shortcut" has you skipping both `generate()` and `calculate()`. Chester and I were talking about switching to requiring `calculate()` to be in there and I wanted to get @beanumber @rudeboybert @mine-cetinkaya-rundel @hardin47 's take.

The rationale for the change is that this syntax doesn't fully parameterize the theoretical distribution. Somewhere in there, the statistic should be specified. A good example is with a 2x2 table, which you could test using p1-p2 or the chisq, and the choice leads to a very different distribution.

The main downside that I see to including `calculate()` is that it kinda muddies up the diagram that I use in my datacamp course that has the shortcut going all the way to `visualize()`. More substantively, it requires users to think of `calculate()` in a different way; right now, a `group_by()`, `summarize()` interpretation works but it won't after this change.

Thoughts?

title: Plans on implementing covariates (e.g., for ANCOVA)?
description: I was wandering if there were plans on implementing *covariates*, for example to allow to compute ANCOVA's on formulas including 3 variables (`outcome ~ predictor + covariate`, for instance in ANCOVA of pre-post/experimental-control experiments: `score_at_posttest ~ condition + score_at_pretest`)?

title: feature request: support for bootstrapping multiple regression models
description:
Two big shifts have taken place in recent years for the intro stats course:
- growth of resampling to simplify inference, and
- increased role of multivariate thinking and multiple regression

We include several weeks on multiple regression, including inference, in our intro stat courses and I know that a number of other institutions do so as well (this is in line with recent curricular guidance, including the revised GAISE College report, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/GAISE/GaiseCollege_Full.pdf).

I really like the infer package approach to inference.  Are there plans to support this use case?  

Just FYI, this is how I would accomplish the task using the mosaic package:

``` r
set.seed(1619)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(mosaic))
coef(lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mtcars))  # observed result
#> (Intercept)          wt         cyl 
#>   39.686261   -3.190972   -1.507795
boots <- mosaic::do(2000) * lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mosaic::resample(mtcars))
mosaic::qdata(~ wt, p = c(.025, .975), data = boots)   # 95% CI for wt coefficient
#>      2.5%     97.5% 
#> -4.958561 -1.945859
```

<sup>Created on 2020-07-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>
```

This is tangentially related to https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/220

```

title: generate vocabulary
description:
Currently the package does three types of `generate()`: `bootstrap`, `permute`, or `simulate`. Every time I teach this I run info difficulties around this vocabulary. `bootstrap` is not problematic but `permute` and `simulate` are hard to distinguish for students.

One other issue is that much of Statistics Education literature refers to these methods as Simulation Based Inference, so having `simulate` as a type of simulation seems odd to me.

A third consideration is that a good portion of the consumers of this package are students in into stat / data science courses where probability is not a requirement. So the difference between permutation / combination may not be clear to them, nor in the learning goals for the course they're taking. Hence, introducing that term makes clearly teaching this material difficult in my experience.

I would like to propose a potentially radical change:

- `generate()` becomes `simulate()`
- `"simulate"` becomes `"draw"` (or `"flip"`, but I think `"draw"` is more general to both numerical and categorical data vs. `"flip"` only makes sense for categorical data to me)
- `"permute"` becomes `"shuffle"`

Discuss 😄 

Obviously we would do this in a non-breaking way via aliasing as opposed to renaming and breaking old code. But I can see the vignettes and teaching materials reading A LOT smoother with these changes.

cc @rudeboybert @mcconvil (when I discussed this with @andrewpbray a while back -- sorry for the delay!! -- he recommended tagging you two as you might have thoughts and feelings on this issue

title: handing of unused factor levels
description:
Because we're currently using the base `chisq.test` to `calculate()` that statistic, bad things happen when one of the variables considered has unused factor levels. This will create, effectively, a row or column of zeroes in the contingency table, which will yield NaNs when trying to compute expected counts. 

Possible solutions:
1. remove our dependence on `chisq.test()` and implement both the vanilla chisq and the one with Yates' continuity correction (which the base function uses). We could fix the expected count of zero thing within that function.
2.  run the data frame through `droplevels()` at the end of `specify()`.

In fact we may want to do both...

Error: Statistic is based on a difference; specify the `order` in which to subtract the levels of the explanatory variable. `order = c("first", "second")` means `("first" - "second")`. Check `?calculate` for details.**

title: Bias corrected and accelerated confidence interval
description: Hello, I noticed that in #237 a bias corrected confidence interval has been added as an option. The current recommenced default is a bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence interval. I would be very interested to see this included. Implementing this would require line 58 in the pull request to be replaced by: `new_probs <- stats::pnorm(0 + (z0 + za / (1 + acc * (z0 + za))))` where `acc` is an additional "acceleration" parameter. The two lines of code generate the same output for `acc = 0` . Unfortunately `acc` cannot be computed from the bootstrap distribution. It is calculated from the original data set using jackknife resampling: The math comes from the book [Computer Age Statistical Inference](https://web.stanford.edu/~hastie/CASI/index.html) pp. 194. So a full implementation would require the original data set to be passed as an argument 'x'. If this was acceptable and stat="mean", say, the theta's in the above math can be calculated as: `thetas = purrr::map(seq_along(x), ~stat::mean(x$response[-.]))` and `acc` can be calculated as: `acc = sum((thetas - stat::mean(thetas))^3) / sum((thetas - stat::mean(thetas))^2)^1.5` / 6. If passing the original data set as an argument is acceptable I would be happy to work towards a pull request? Matt

title: Avoid crash BY MEMORY OVERFLOW the generate step with map
description:
That is just a hack but not a perfect solution.

Sometimes, when you need to sample data, depending on your system memory, size of the data, and the number of replicates, you may get a crash by out-of-memory (maybe caused by memory limit set in Rstudio?).

like:
```
tmpdf %>%
  specify(sbp_commu ~ st2tm_commu) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "Chisq") -> ts_chi_per
```

Might be converted to this:

```
1:1000 %>% 
  map(
    function(x){
      tmpdf %>%
        specify(sbp_commu ~ st2tm_commu) %>%
        generate(reps = 1, type = "bootstrap") %>%
        calculate(stat = "Chisq")
    }

  bind_rows() %>% 
  rownames_to_column(var = "replicate") %>% 
  mutate(replicate = as.integer(replicate)) -> ts_chi_bs
```

Avoiding out-of-memory for somewhy. 

The proper way to deal with it might be by calculating stat just after you generate a sample, one by one.

If there is another method that I don't know, please, let me know.

title: Should `alternative` or `direction` be within `hypothesise()`?
description:
In a classical hypothesis test, you are supposed to specify the direction of the alternative in the hypothesis. 

Therefore I wonder if there should there be a `direction` or `alternative` argument within `hypothesise`, instead of `direction` arguments within `shade_p_value` & `get_p_value`.

I think the term `alternative` is nicer in the hypothesis function, as it reads clearer about what it relates to. 

This issue also relates to #378 

Great R package btw!

Currently like this:
```r
obs_stat <- gss %>%
  specify(response = hours) %>%
  hypothesise(null = "point", mu = 40) %>%
  calculate(stat = "t") 

null_distribution <- gss %>%
  specify(response = hours) %>%
  hypothesise(null = "point", mu = 40) %>%
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "t")

null_distribution %>% 
  visualise(method = "both") + 
  shade_p_value(obs_stat, direction = "two-sided")

null_distribution %>% 
  get_p_value(obs_stat, direction = "two-sided")
```

Instead could be like this:
```r
obs_stat <- gss %>%
  specify(response = hours) %>%
  hypothesise(null = "point", mu = 40, alternative = "two-sided") %>%
  calculate(stat = "t") 

null_distribution <- gss %>%
  specify(response = hours) %>%
  hypothesise(null = "point", mu = 40, alternative = "two-sided") %>%
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "t")

null_distribution %>% 
  visualise(method = "both") + 
  shade_p_value(obs_stat)

null_distribution %>% 
  get_p_value(obs_stat)
```

title: Inconsistent warning in two-sided hypothesis test for difference in proportions on factor vs character variables
description:
Hi,

I came across the following inconsistency when performing 2-sided hypothesis tests for difference in proportions. When the explanatory variable is coded as a factor, adding the `shade_p_value` layer produces the warning message “Chi-Square usually corresponds to right-tailed tests. Proceed with caution.” However, when performing the same test with the explanatory variable coded as a character vector, no such warning appears. This warning message may be particularly perplexing to the intended audience of the `infer` package, since it may not be immediately clear why a chi-square test is being used for difference in proportion. Moreover, the message does not appear if the variable is coded as a character vector, and the distinction between character and factor may be unclear to the new user.

Reprex:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
data(gss)

#####partyid coded as factor

gss_rd <- gss %>%  filter(partyid %in% c("rep", "dem"))

class(gss_rd$partyid)

gss_null<-gss_rd %>% specify(college ~ partyid, success = "degree") %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% 
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>% 
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("rep", "dem")) 

gss_stat <- gss_rd %>% specify(college ~ partyid, success = "degree") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("rep", "dem")) 

gss_null %>% visualise()+shade_p_value(obs_stat = gss_stat, direction = "both")

#####partyid coded as character vector

gss_rd <- gss %>%  filter(partyid %in% c("rep", "dem")) %>% mutate(partyid = as.character(partyid) )

class(gss_rd$partyid)

gss_null<-gss_rd %>% specify(college ~ partyid, success = "degree") %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% 
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>% 
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("rep", "dem")) 

gss_stat <- gss_rd %>% specify(college ~ partyid, success = "degree") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("rep", "dem")) 

gss_null %>% visualise()+shade_p_value(obs_stat = gss_stat, direction = "both")
```

title: Refactor `rep_sample_n()` and `rep_slice_sample()`
description:
Having reviewed code for both `rep_sample_n()` and `rep_slice_sample()`, I believe it would be beneficial if they get refactored to be a direct wrappers for `dplyr::sample_n()` and `dplyr::slice_sample()`. To certain extent it was a [suggested implementation](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/pull/325/commits/8f9d7b7fd7de3ca47f6c336332214319a02f2922) (adapted from [this suggestion](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/279#issuecomment-663091620)) when `rep_slice_sample()` was introduced. I [decided](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/pull/325#pullrequestreview-455277831) to keep the original implementation in order to avoid using really fresh {dplyr}'s `slice_sample()`.

Now I believe that decision was not a poor choice in the long term. Here is why:

- As I understand it, the goal of `rep_*()` functions is to be a direct extensions of {dplyr}'s counterparts. If so, those {dplyr} functions should be used directly: `sample_n()` in `rep_sample_n()` and `slice_sample()` in `rep_slice_sample()`. Even if it means breaking some current behavior, this should simplify cognitive load on both users and maintainers. However, this also means that if those functions change their arguments (add, rename, etc.), it should be mirrored in the `rep_*()` functions.
- Fixing #361 would have been a much more straightforward job (the need of having complexity of #362 is a clear evidence). By the way, this suggestion also means that `prop` argument shouldn't be added to `rep_sample_n()` as there is no such argument in `dplyr::sample_n()`.

@ismayc , @simonpcouch , what are your thoughts on this?

title: Add prop argument to rep_slice_sample()
description: It's useful when bootstrapping to specify a `prop` argument instead of the number of rows if keeping things basic and not getting into the {infer} pipeline. This was requested on the {moderndive} package [here](https://github.com/moderndive/moderndive/issues/98), but since we import `rep_sample_n()` from {infer} we probably should import `rep_slice_sample()` as well. We'd prefer to not have two different versions of the same function floating around (one with `prop` and one without).

title: Do NAs get resampled?
description: The `calculate` function takes the `na.rm` argument for the statistic it's calculating. But does this mean at the generate stage, say if we're doing a bootstrap interval, `NA`s from the original sample get resampled? If so, I believe this is not a good idea. Because chances are when we look at the sample size for the original sample those NAs don't factor into it. And a bootstrap sample should be the same size as the original sample. If indeed the `NA`s from the original sample don't make it into the bootstrap samples, then isn't the `na.rm` argument in calculate unnecessary?

This will help to clear up the number of things we are working on at any given time and help us prioritize what is next using the `develop` branch, which won't differ much from the `master` branch, encouraging more PRs and tweaks. Does anyone else have experience with a release schedule like this? @beanumber @andrewpbray @mine-cetinkaya-rundel @rudeboybert?

title: Hypothesize function
description:
**Proposed input**: dataframe/tibble that has already been `select()`ed down to variables of interest.
**Proposted output**: tibble with a flag for the null hypothesis selected, similar to `group_by()`

I like the idea of having students specify a `null` argument here, probably in the form of a character string. Deciding how to describe each of the null's we want will be difficult. I took a stab at them in the examples in the README, but I have lots of questions:

1. Should parameters show up in these?
2.  Should there be any reference to the columns in the data frame that comes in or should we be doing checks of types within the function?
3. Will we rerun into problems when going back and forth between the computational and approximation versions of a particular test? That is, are there cases where the null hypotheses aren't exactly the same?
4. Should we add an argument for `alternative`? My sense right now is no - that the goal of this is the `visualize()`ation of the sampling distribution. We could always write a `p-value()` function that has an `alternate` argument.

title: naming of functions
description: Instead of `generate()` with different types, would it be better to have `simulate()`, `bootstrap()` and `permute()` just be separate functions? They are "verbs" after all... Wouldn't this make it even clearer what is happening?

title: Generate function
description:
**Proposed input**: a tibble with some meta-info from `hypothesize()`
**Proposed output**: a much taller tibble that is the input `repeat()`ed n times along with an indexing column.

This function is pretty much the same as Mine's `rep_sample_n()` and it encapsulates the idea that the null hypothesis should encode some mechanism by which you can generate additional data sets under that null hypothesis. Some thoughts/questions:

- Right now, the only argument I'm thinking of is `repeat()` for the number of iterations. The meta-info that's appended with `hypothesize()` should be sufficient to know whether this is a permutation or simulation situation.
- This function could also be called `simulate()`.
- If we want this to package to be scalable to larger data sets and still run fairly fast, we might want to write some backup functionality here. As in: if the data set is really big, hold off on spooling out 1000 copies of it in memory. We can probably be more efficient about that if we don't need to show this repeated data set as output here.

title: Still think the parameters for a multi-level factor should be a vector
description:
Especially since they are going to get passed to the `prob` argument of `sample()`, which is already a vector.

```
prob	
A vector of probability weights for obtaining the elements of the vector being sampled.
```

title: Print methods
description:
I'd like people to be able to break the inferential pipeline at anypoint and have the output make sense. The default tibble/data.frames that we're working in are pretty good, but there are other attributes related to `hypothesize()` that would be nice to print (similar to how "Groups: cyl" will be printed at the top of the output of `group_by(mtcars, cyl)`.

Seems like all we'd need to do to do this is add an `infer` class to the dataframe then make a print method that will supercede that of `tbl` and `data.frame`. I was hoping to just tweak the existing print methods for that but...I've been having a tough time tracking them down. They appear to be in `tibble`, but I haven't gotten much more than learning about `format()` and `trunc_mat()`.

Has anyone been able to find them?

title: Use tidyeval functionality
description:
This is relevant to `calculate` but maybe others too, if any of those use underscore verbs from dplyr, which is now deprecated functionality.

Prototype for calculating for `stat == "mean"`

```r
  if (stat == "mean") {
    col <- setdiff(names(x), "replicate")
    x %>%
      dplyr::group_by(replicate) %>%
      dplyr::summarize(stat = mean(!!sym(col)))
  }
```

Note that this requires importing the `sym` function from the rlang package, which dplyr currently does not import automatically.

Is someone up for updating the calculate function with this, or should I? We also need to resolve #15 and #16 to and all of the updates can be done at once.

title: Calculate should not use `mean` as the var name in output
description:
This is in the summarise step of calculate. Since `mean` is a function it's not good practice to also use it as variable name, same with median etc. Alternatives:

1. Generically call all of them `stat` so the output looks the same regardless of what statistic is used, this means user has to remember which it was, which is ok I think since in the function call they specify it.
    - If we go with this we can add a note to the output saying "stat is mean" or "stat is diff in means"  something like that, but at least the variable name stays the same which is nice for subsequent calculations or visualizations.
2. Use names like "boot_mean", "boot_median", etc. Or some other prefix.

My vote is for Option 1.

Another thing I do in my course is to create a sampling distribution of slopes taken from a huge population.  I do this in chapter 1 before I've done any inference.  The idea is just to visualize how the slopes change from sample to sample *outside* the context of making specific hypotheses.

group_by(replicate) %>%

filter(term=="explanatory")

```

title: How do you plan to support tests in the context of lm() and glm()?
description:
As @nicholasjorton suggested, it will be important to be able to move easily beyond the traditional Intro Stats tests to this more flexible space -- else you are just a dead end.

Perhaps it would be better to start from that end than from the 1- and 2-sample end.  Most of the 1- and 2-sample things can be thought of as special cases of this more general setting anyway.

title: open or closed system?
description:
I've gone at least quickly through all the issues now.  It seems like you are trying to create a very closed system -- users will only be able to conduct hypothesis tests that you have imagined in advance they will want to do to and for which they know the magic character strings that name the test.  This is only marginally different from having a separate function for each test.

A true grammar of hypothesis testing would be a more open system where a new hypothesis test could be conducted without needing to add to the package.

For starters, in `calculate()`, why isn't `stat` a function (or a string that names a function).  That would allow users to use any test statistic by providing a function of the proper arity for the data.  It would also allow users to directly apply the stat function to the data set in question to get the observed value of the test statistic.

Here are some test cases for your "grammar":

  * how do I test that two medians are the same using the difference in medians as a test statistic?
  * ditto for other quantiles
  * how do I test that 2 groups have the same variance using the difference in standard deviations as a test statistic?
  * how do I test that 3 groups have the same variance using the variance of the variances as a test statistic?

description:
Running `?calculate`, the example works:
```

library(tidyverse)

Happy to do a PR but wanted to see (1) am I interpreting current status correctly and (2) is everyone on board with a new `order` argument that will be something like `order = c("level1" - "level2")` which translates to `mean(y[x == "level1"]) - mean(y[x == "level2"])`.

title: Student/teaching experience with generate type
description:
I'm using `infer` in my in-class teaching this semester, and I can't yet definitively say how learning is going, but in general based on informal observation, seems ok.

However one type of question I've been getting repeatedly is "How do I know when to use which type for generating samples?". This is a good question of course, and the answer leads us to discussing differences. But what I'm observing is that students are trying to make if this then that type lists (like if I have categorical variable and point null then simulate). And what's worrisome about it is that it feels a bit like the cheatsheets students put together in courses that teach theoretical inference with type of tests and SE formulas. One of the main motivations for coming up with consistent syntax was to move away from such thinking.

Have others using this in in-class teaching experienced this? Any thoughts? @andrewpbray @beanumber @hardin47

Note: The one alternative I can think of is to have the package decide the type of generate based on the info that comes before it. This is similar to how it worked in my `inference` function. But it hides what I *think* is an important detail. Unfortunately my limited experience in showing that detail hasn't been super positive, but I'm willing to accept that's the way to go, just wanted to hear from others what they think after having students use these functions.

title: Only have monochromatic bins in null distribution + p-value histograms?
description:
In the [Randomization approach to t-statistic](https://infer.netlify.com/articles/two_sample_t.html#randomization-approach-to-t-statistic) example: 
```
library(nycflights13)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(infer)
set.seed(2017)

# Create data frame
fli_small <- flights %>% 
  sample_n(size = 500) %>% 
  mutate(half_year = case_when(
    between(month, 1, 6) ~ "h1",
    between(month, 7, 12) ~ "h2"
  )) %>% 
  mutate(day_hour = case_when(
    between(hour, 1, 12) ~ "morning",
    between(hour, 13, 24) ~ "not morning"
  )) %>% 
  select(arr_delay, dep_delay, half_year, 
         day_hour, origin, carrier)

# Null
obs_t <- fli_small %>% 
  t_stat(formula = arr_delay ~ half_year)
t_null_distn <- fli_small %>%
  specify(arr_delay ~ half_year) %>% # alt: response = arr_delay, explanatory = half_year
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "t")
t_null_distn %>% 
  visualize(obs_stat = obs_t, direction = "two_sided")
```
I think having the bin that straddles the test-statistic value (and its negative) have two colors will definitely trip novices out. Is there anyway to have two bin boundaries be the test statistic value (and its negative) by default, so that we have monochromatic bins? And only if people specify a particular `bin`/`binwidth`, resort to this two-color binning scheme?

title: Success should always be defined
description:
In working on a solution for #53 I realized that if `success` isn't defined by the user we make an assumption and use the first level as success. I don't think this is a good approach because it makes the function "just work" without the student properly formulating the inference chain. I propose removing https://github.com/andrewpbray/infer/blob/f034a8629dd42c83d4fbb33dd1b80324262dbb12/R/calculate.R#L60 and https://github.com/andrewpbray/infer/blob/f034a8629dd42c83d4fbb33dd1b80324262dbb12/R/calculate.R#L61 and instead throwing an error saying success must be defined when the response variable is categorical. I can put that in the same PR as the `order` solution.

Also, as far as I can tell currently the `"diff in props"` example isn't working since `success` functionality isn't built into the difference in proportions case (only the single proportion).

This is relevant to the discussion in #54 about using `type = "simulate"` being confusing in `generate()`.

title: Do we need an infer class?
description:
I noticed that we're inconsistent in how we perpetuate the `infer` class, as demo'ed below.

```
library(tidyverse)
library(forcats)
library(infer)
s <- gss_cat %>%
         specify(marital ~ race)
h <- s %>%
         hypothesize(null = "independence")
g <- h %>%
         generate(g, reps = 6, type = "permute")
cal <- g %>%
        calculate(g, stat = "Chisq")
class(s)
# [1] "infer"      "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
class(h)
# [1] "infer"      "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
class(g)
# [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
class(cal)
# [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
```

The class is tacked on the way out the door in specify(), is perpetuated through `hypothesize()`, then get's lost when we take things apart and put them back together in `generate()`.

Do we need this class? The only advantage I can think of right now is if we wanted to replace `visualize()` with a plot method, but it seems messy to use a base R function that will output a `ggplot`. Maybe there's a reason that its bad practice to tack extra attributes onto tibbles without indicating an additional class? Any advice on this @sckott?

title: var.equal in `t_stat`
description:
Hello,

I'm trying to use `t_stat` to get the t-statistic on the assumption that the two variances are equal. I had assumed that passing in `var.equal = TRUE` via `...` would do the trick, but it doesn't appear to make a difference (the statistic remains the same as before, assuming unequal variances). I've also tried this using `specify` and then `calculate`. Am I missing something, or is this a bug? 

Here's a reproducible example, following on from the vignette:

```{r}
library(nycflights13)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(infer)
set.seed(2017)
fli_small <- flights %>% 
  sample_n(size = 500) %>% 
  mutate(half_year = case_when(
    between(month, 1, 6) ~ "h1",
    between(month, 7, 12) ~ "h2"
  )) %>% 
  mutate(day_hour = case_when(
    between(hour, 1, 12) ~ "morning",
    between(hour, 13, 24) ~ "not morning"
  )) %>% 
  select(arr_delay, dep_delay, half_year, 
         day_hour, origin, carrier)

obs_t <- fli_small %>% 
  t_stat(formula = arr_delay ~ half_year, order = c("h1", "h2"))

obs_t_equal <- fli_small %>% 
  t_stat(formula = arr_delay ~ half_year, order = c("h1", "h2"), var.equal = TRUE)

obs_t == obs_t_equal # TRUE - SHOULD BE FALSE

# compare with t.test
h1_vec <- fli_small %>%
  filter(half_year == "h1") %>%
  pull(arr_delay)

h2_vec <- fli_small %>%
  filter(half_year == "h2") %>%
  pull(arr_delay)

obs_t_stats <- t.test(h1_vec, h2_vec)$statistic

obs_t_equal_stats <- t.test(h1_vec, h2_vec, var.equal = TRUE)$statistic

obs_t_stats == obs_t_equal_stats # FALSE - as should be

obs_t_stats == obs_t # TRUE - as should be

obs_t_equal_stats == obs_t_equal # FALSE - SHOULD BE TRUE
```

title: Using 'assertive' introduces unnecessary dependencies
description:
Recently I installed `infer` for the first time and noticed that this also got 16 (sixteen!) other `assertive.*` packages installed. Those now occupy most of the 'Packages' tab when I open it. This is (weirdly) somewhat annoying as I have to do extra scrolling to get to the package I need.

After studying internal code I saw that `assertive` is only used for checking types of input arguments. In other words, it is not crucial for the package logic but rather a convenient implementation choice. I can offer to change this implementation to one of the following:

1. **Use `assertive.types` package directly**. This reduces number of `assertive.*` packages to 2 and is enough for current code. However, other assertion types may introduce the need for other `assertive.*` packages.
1. **Use some other (more generic) package for type checks**. I can recommend [checkmate](https://mllg.github.io/checkmate/index.html) for this. This reduces number of extra packages to constant 2 (`checkmate` and its dependency `backports`). It is also flexible, easy to use and extend, and has built-in functions for all current type checks (right now no extending is needed). Error messages are very similar to `assertive`: both provide present and needed types:

    ``` r
    x <- TRUE

    assertive::assert_is_numeric(x)
    #> Error: is_numeric : x is not of class 'numeric'; it has class 'logical'.

    checkmate::assert_numeric(x)
    #> Error in checkmate::assert_numeric(x): Assertion on 'x' failed: Must be of type 'numeric', not 'logical'.
    ```
 
1. **Write own assertion functions**. For the current code not much work is needed to implement this. The distinctive advantage of this approach is the ability to customize error messages: for example, remove those "Error ..." in the beginning. No extra packages are needed for this option (`rlang` should be enough).

I am wondering the following:

- Would you be interested in PR regarding updating assertions implementation?
- If yes, which type of change would you prefer?

title: Format documentation to follow tidyverse style guide
description:
I have a suggestion to format current documentation to be closer to [tidyverse style guide](http://style.tidyverse.org/documentation.html). This (rather long) comment is going to show which format changes I think should be done to increase readability of documentation code. As some of them are matter of taste, this issue is created for discussion of this suggestion. Slightly modified version of [`get_pvalue()` documentation](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/e756b679b63de9a8a0aae617e04a2ceb2cb5f1f7/R/p_value.R#L1) will be an example for cumulative changes (shown in collapsable spoilers):
Current documentation ```r #' Compute the p-value for (currently only) simulation-based methods #' \code{get_pvalue()} is an alias of \code{p_value} #' @param x data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes #' of theoretical distribution values #' @param obs_stat a numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more extreme than this) #' @param direction a character string. Options are "less", "greater", or "two_sided". #' Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return a 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1 #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue get_pvalue <- p_value ```

**Step 1: Use markdown**. Not many changes here, but documentation with more inline code and cross-linking will benefit from that.
After using markdown ```r #' Compute the p-value for (currently only) simulation-based methods #' `get_pvalue()` is an alias of `p_value`. #' @param x data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes #' of theoretical distribution values #' @param obs_stat a numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more extreme than this) #' @param direction a character string. Options are "less", "greater", or "two_sided". #' Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return a 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1 #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue get_pvalue <- p_value ```

**Step 2: Reflow roxygen comments**. Use width of 80 characters, as this goes along with recommendation for syntax and spares the need for horizontal scroll in IDE. New lines should be indented by two spaces. Alternatively, tags that span over multiple lines (like `@description`, `@examples` and `@section`) can have the corresponding tag on its own line and then subsequent lines don’t need to be indented (see [this guide section](http://style.tidyverse.org/documentation.html#indents-and-line-breaks)). Use maximum allowed width. If output text will be shown as one line, it should be on one line in source too. Usually, this step can be done by using `Ctrl+Shift+/` shortcut in RStudio (complicated nested list is one exception). It will be good if code in examples is also under tidyverse style. In this case it means to use indentation of two spaces instead of four.
After reflow ```r #' Compute the p-value for (currently only) simulation-based methods #' `get_pvalue()` is an alias of `p_value`. #' @param x data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes of #' theoretical distribution values #' @param obs_stat a numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more #' extreme than this) #' @param direction a character string. Options are "less", "greater", or #' "two_sided". Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return a 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1 #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @export #' @rdname get_pvalue get_pvalue <- p_value ```

**Step 3: Arrange documentation blocks**. Mostly used "blocks" are: title, description, parameters, details, extra sections, return value, "See also", examples, and development-target. All blocks should be separated by line break. After documentation code there should be a documented object (without line break). By "development-target block" I mean a set of roxygen keywrods that don't directly appear in documentation: `@export`, `@name`, `importFrom`, etc. I prefer to stick to this order of "blocks", however it is not mandatory. The one thing I really prefer is to have development-target block right in the end, which is usually right near the function. Also `@export` should come last to easily see whether the object is exported. Also this step seems like a nice time to ensure that title is as short as it can be, moving the rest to description.
After arranging blocks ```r #' Compute the p-value #' #' P-value is implemented for (currently only) simulation-based methods. #' `get_pvalue()` is an alias of `p_value`. #' #' @param x data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes of #' theoretical distribution values #' @param obs_stat a numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more #' extreme than this) #' @param direction a character string. Options are "less", "greater", or #' "two_sided". Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return a 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1 #' #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) #' #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @export p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @export get_pvalue <- p_value ```

**Step 4: Use sentence case with full stop (except in title)**.
After sentence case ```r #' Compute the p-value #' #' P-value is implemented for (currently only) simulation-based methods. #' `get_pvalue()` is an alias of `p_value`. #' #' @param x Data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes of #' theoretical distribution values. #' @param obs_stat A numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more #' extreme than this). #' @param direction A character string. Options are "less", "greater", or #' "two_sided". Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return A 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1. #' #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) #' #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @export p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @rdname get_pvalue #' @export get_pvalue <- p_value ```

**Step 5: Use `@name` to document multiple objects**. Documentation should be done for `NULL` with setting an informative `@name`. This isn't really a tidyverse guide but rather an option in [this section](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/roxygen2/vignettes/rd.html#documenting-multiple-functions-in-the-same-file) of `roxygen2` vignette. I like this way because it forces to think about an explicit name for a set of documented objects. Notes: - The way of "documenting `NULL`" forces to place `@export` tag near all documented functions. It shouldn't be placed in main documentation code. - If name differs from names of all objects, extra help page will be created in the package index. This step is pretty arguable, so please tell your thoughts.
Final result ```r #' Compute the p-value #' #' P-value is implemented for (currently only) simulation-based methods. #' `get_pvalue()` is an alias of `p_value`. #' #' @param x Data frame of calculated statistics or containing attributes of #' theoretical distribution values. #' @param obs_stat A numeric value or a 1x1 data frame (as extreme or more #' extreme than this). #' @param direction A character string. Options are "less", "greater", or #' "two_sided". Can also specify "left", "right", or "both". #' #' @return A 1x1 data frame with value between 0 and 1. #' #' @examples #' mtcars_df <- mtcars %>% #' dplyr::mutate(am = factor(am)) #' #' @name p_value NULL #' @rdname p_value #' @export p_value <- function(x, obs_stat, direction) {x} #' @rdname p_value #' @export get_pvalue <- p_value ```

That's probably it. There is also a matter of indentation inside a nested list (I prefer to indent all text in list node equally). However, there seem to be no nested lists in documentation yet, so it is not urgent. Questions: 1. In style guide there is a suggestion to "not use code font for package names". So in documentation instead of "`infer`" there should be "infer package". I don'y really like this one. There are also options like "{infer}" (saw in this package couple of times) and "'infer'" (CRAN guide). Which one is preferred? I like using "{infer}" but it means writing "\\{infer\\}" in documentation code. title: Format code to follow tidyverse style guide
Make code more DRY
description:
After reading {infer} code I noticed that some code chunks are repeated multiple times with, possibly, small changes. This seems like a good opportunity to abstract them into functions to facilitate code reusage and increase code stability (see [DRY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don%27t_repeat_yourself)). I created this issue to track those code chunks.

- Methods of `calc_impl` for one function, like [this one](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/43a1119bc942be344638a203b535861cb9060179/R/calculate.R#L129). They can be abstracted into `calc_impl_one_f(fun)` that returns appropriate functions.
- Methods of `calc_impl` for difference, like [this one](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/43a1119bc942be344638a203b535861cb9060179/R/calculate.R#L207). As in previous one, can be abstracted into `calc_impl_diff_f(fun)`.
- `is.null(attr(x, at))`. As this code is repeated many, many times I think it is better to create `is_nuat(x, at)` function to replace it.
- Copying attributes from one object to another, for example [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/43a1119bc942be344638a203b535861cb9060179/R/calculate.R#L286). This is currently done with [set_attributes()](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/develop/R/utils.R#L12), but I think it should be renamed to `copy_attrs(to, from, attr_vec)` and have `attr_vec` as argument.
- Create separate `helper-data.R` file in `tests/testthat` with initializations of data that is used across multiple test files. For example, [iris_tbl](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/43a1119bc942be344638a203b535861cb9060179/tests/testthat/test-calculate.R#L5) and [mtcars](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/43a1119bc942be344638a203b535861cb9060179/tests/testthat/test-generate.R#L3) (which probably should be renamed to `mtcars_tbl`). This file will be sourced by {testthat} before any 'test-*.R' files and results can be used in tests.

If this is considered worthwhile, I plan to make a PR with corresponding changes at the end of this week. Please, add here any thoughts about possibilities of reducing code duplication. Special attention might be devoted to predicates inside `if`, as there are a lot of them.

title: Have any summary function work in calculate
description:
I really like using The Lady Tasting Tea to motivate hypothesis testing. The following code does the trick:
```
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
lady_tasting_tea <- data_frame(
  first = as.factor(c(rep("milk",4), rep("tea",4)))
  )

lady_tasting_tea %>%
  specify(response = first) %>% # alt: am ~ NULL (or am ~ 1)
  hypothesize(null = "point", p = c("milk" = .5, "tea" = .5)) %>% 
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "simulate") %>% 
  calculate(stat = "prop")
```
However, it would be great if the final stat could be "sum". That way there is one less layer of abstraction between the experiment and the null distribution (students can read off count directly, instead of reading off proportions)

In a more general setting, any many-to-one summary function would be great, for example all those that work with `dplyr::summarize()`

title: Clarify calculated "t" statistic versus Welch's t
description:
Hi!

I'm using {infer} in class and noticed something while teaching two-sample t-tests that I think might be good to clarify in the documentation, or perhaps may involve a slight edit to the API for `calculate`. I tried to do a `reprex` with a mini sample of observations but no matter what my t-statistic and Welch's t ended up being the exact same so I am just including the whole data to show the issue I am seeing (sorry for the length- I tried!).

So my issue is that the t and Welch's t with this data differ. Using `t_test`, I got the results I expected based on `t.test` with the `var.equal` argument. But in the {infer} pipeline using `specify() %>% calculate()`, I seem to only be able to calculate Welch's t statistic (it ignores the `var.equal = TRUE` argument). This got me thinking that some users may unwittingly do a permutation t-test with Welch's t-statistic. This probably makes little practical difference, but may be worth noting in the docs. 

Alternatively, I could see it being helpful to have one of the possible `stats` that can be `calculate()`d be `welch-t`, or have a required argument when selecting `stat = "t"` for `var.equal` as with the base `t.test`. Anyway, just some ideas, thanks for the great package 😄

title: Deprecate the unnecessary function aliasses
description:
I think that having multiple names for the same function makes things harder, not easier, to understand.  For example, `get_confidence_interval()`, `get_ci()`, and`conf_int()` are all identical. 

I'd be tempted to keep `get_confidence_interval()` and deprecate the other two.

Likewise, there is no point in having `get_pvalue()` *and* `p_value()`.

Aliases make it harder to read other people's code, since you need to understand the other coder's dialect as well as your own.

title: Handling of argument `type` in `generate()`
description:
Having studied code of `generate()`, I have a question about the logic of how it handles `type` argument.

The current approach accounts for two scenarios:

- **`x` already has "type" attribute set**. In that case, `generate()` double checks that user supplied *the same* value and throws error if he/she didn't. If values are the same, it reassigns `type` to be equal to the value of "type" attribute (which it already equals).
- **`x` doesn't have "type" attribute set**. In that case, use supplied `type`. In this scenario it doesn't create attribute "type" which is, in my opinion, not good.

This encouraged me to suggest the following flow:

- **If user wants to use default** (i.e. the one already supplied in attribute) **generation type, it is used**. This is usually done by supplying `NULL`. If desired attribute is not present, error should be thrown.
- **If user wants to use own type, let him/her**:
    - Possibly warn that supplied type differs from already present one.
    - Check that it is a valid type (one of the "bootstrap", "permute", "simulate").
    - Set attribute "type" to the supplied `type`.

The extra benefit of this flow is that the default value of `type` is `NULL` and not `attr(x, "type")` (which might be puzzling to users).

What was the original cause to choose the current approach?

title: Refactor visualization
description:
This is somewhat a continuation of #173. Even after DRYing `visualize()` in #177 I think it can be further refactored to be more straightforward. In my understanding, the visualizaion algorithm should be as follows:

1. **Check inputs for type and reasonability correctness**. This is a step that shouldn't repair any inputs but only throw errors, warnings, and messages. It includes [type checks](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/81402ba402897c9ec8e00529e7ed7e9f81262d84/R/visualize.R#L82-L98) and [attention warnings](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/81402ba402897c9ec8e00529e7ed7e9f81262d84/R/visualize.R#L153-L160).
1. **Initialize the plot**. It can be done with either `ggplot()` or `ggplot(data)` based on the later design (probably second one is better).
1. **Add simulation layer**:
    - If `method = "simulation"` then this is a `geom_histogram()` or `geom_bar()` of `stat` column (choice is based on number of its unique elements).
    - If `method = "theoretical"` then no layer is added.
    - If `method = "both"` then this is a `geom_histogram()` of `stat` column and `aes(y = ..density..)`.
1. **Add theoretical layer**:
    - If `method = "simulation"` then no layer is added.
    - If `method = "theoretical"` then output of `stat_function()` is returned [in the range between \[0.001, 0.999\]](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/81402ba402897c9ec8e00529e7ed7e9f81262d84/R/visualize.R#L203) quantiles of theoretical distribution from `attr(data, "theory_type")`.
    - If `method = "both"` then output of `stat_function()` is returned based on the range of `stat` column (as [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/81402ba402897c9ec8e00529e7ed7e9f81262d84/R/visualize.R#L227)).
1. **Add external statistics**. It seems that current `develop` and `master` versions of the code is intended to prohibit simultaneous usage of observed statistic `obs_stat` and interval data `endpoints`. For now it has some flaws as just supplying them both without shading gives a warning "Values for both `endpoints` and `obs_stat` were given when only one should be set. Ignoring `obs_stat` values." and then plots both objects with vertical lines. For me personally it was a surprise that I can't plot both of them, but I somewhat understand the motivation of not mixing p-values with confidence intervals. I strongly suggest to change their plotting in one of the following ways:
    1. *Treat value and shading as a whole*. Most declared features will be present. If both `obs_stat` and `end_points` are present, give a warning and use only `endpoints` (no vertical line and shading is done for `obs_stat`).
    1. *Create new function to add external statistics to `ggplot` object*. It can be of the form `add_external_stat(stat1, stat2 = NULL, line_col = "red2", direction = NULL, shadow_fill = "pink")`. If one statistic is supplied, plot as currently with p-value. If two - as with `endpoints`. The biggest benefit of this approach is that `visualize()` will have far less arguments and be easier to use. The downside is the need to manually change the color if both p-value and CI data are plotted.
    1. *Create two separate functions for adding p-value and CI data to plot*. I prefer this option as it is more targeted, explicit, allows comfotable defaults, and still lighten `visualize()` arguments. They can be `add_pvalue(value, color = "red2", fill = "pink", direction = NULL)` and `add_ci(endpoints, color = "mediumaquamarine", fill = "turquoise")`.
1. **Add title and labels**.
    - Title is constructed based on the `method` and type of theoretical distribution.
    - Y label is either "count" (for `method = "simulation"`) or "density".
    - X label is `stat` for `method = "simulation"` and `<short distr name> stat` where \<short distr name\> is taken from [this function](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/81402ba402897c9ec8e00529e7ed7e9f81262d84/R/visualize.R#L520).

title: expect_warning() on old windows builds
description:
En route to CRAN, the `develop` branch is not passing the check against old windows builds (a recurring issue).  It looks like the problem boils down to an error from `expect_warning()` in several of the tests, the ones that generate > 1 warnings.  The message is `the condition has length > 1`, when `expect_warning()` is run on the output below.

``` r
library(infer)
library(testthat)

mtcars_df <- mtcars %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    cyl = factor(cyl), vs = factor(vs), am = factor(am), gear = factor(gear),
    carb = factor(carb)
  )

mtcars_df %>%
  specify(cyl ~ NULL) %>% # alt: response = cyl
  hypothesize(
    null = "point", p = c("4" = .5, "6" = .25, "8" = .25)
  ) %>%
  generate(reps = 100, type = "bootstrap")
#> Warning: You have given `type = "bootstrap"`, but `type` is expected to be
#> `"simulate"`. This workflow is untested and the results may not mean what
#> you think they mean.
#> Warning in if (attr(attr(x, "params"), "names") == "mu") {: the condition
#> has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
#> Warning in if (attr(attr(x, "params"), "names") == "med") {: the condition
#> has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
#> Response: cyl (factor)
#> Null Hypothesis: point
#> # A tibble: 3,200 x 2
#> # Groups:   replicate [100]
#>    replicate cyl  
#>        <int> <fct>
#>  1         1 8    
#>  2         1 4    
#>  3         1 8    
#>  4         1 8    
#>  5         1 8    
#>  6         1 4    
#>  7         1 8    
#>  8         1 8    
#>  9         1 6    
#> 10         1 8    
#> # ... with 3,190 more rows
```
Created on 2018-11-12 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

In trying to sew this up, I'm reminded of a message that someone from R core sent out about a year ago announcing a change to the way conditions handle vectors, which might be the reason for the current error. Does this sound familiar to anyone?

`expect_warnings()` can take as a second argument a RegEx describing the warning message, so we could hard code the first warning to placate it, but it’d make the whole thing brittler than it should be. We could also shift the first warning to an error so that the other two warnings never occur, but it really should be a warning here.

Any ideas for how to fix this more permanently?

Debugging through `build_win()` is torture.

title: Which variable to resample for inference about the regression slope?
description:
Hello, I would like to infer about the slope for the following model using openintro's [evals](https://www.openintro.org/stat/data/evals.php) data: 
> teaching_score = beta_0 + beta_1 * avg_beauty_score  

Take a look at the reprex below that performs one replicate of a permutation test
``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(moderndive)
library(infer)

# Select subset of variables
data("evals")
evals <- evals %>% 
  select(score, bty_avg)

# Unpermuted original data:
evals %>% 
  slice(2:9)
#> # A tibble: 8 x 2
#>   score bty_avg
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1   4.1    5   
#> 2   3.9    5   
#> 3   4.8    5   
#> 4   4.6    3   
#> 5   4.3    3   
#> 6   2.8    3   
#> 7   4.1    3.33
#> 8   3.4    3.33

# One replicate of permutation:
evals %>% 
  specify(score ~ bty_avg) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>% 
  generate(reps = 1) %>% 
  slice(2:9)
#> Setting `type = "permute"` in `generate()`.
#> # A tibble: 8 x 3
#> # Groups:   replicate [1]
#>   score bty_avg replicate
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>     <int>
#> 1   4.6    5            1
#> 2   4.6    5            1
#> 3   4.2    5            1
#> 4   3.3    3            1
#> 5   4.1    3            1
#> 6   4.1    3            1
#> 7   4.5    3.33         1
#> 8   4.9    3.33         1
```
I noticed that it is the response variable `y = score` that is permuted, not the explanatory variable `x = bty_avg`.

**Question**: Was permuting the `y` and not the `x` by design? If so, could you let me know why? Because I feel that permuting the `x` makes more sense, as this is the "treatment" variable whose associated effect we want to study under the null hypothesis.

This question might just be an exercise in philosophical pedantry, since materially for simple linear regression it makes no difference which variable you permute. However if we wanted to extend these ideas to multiple regression in theory (if not in practice in the `infer` package) then you definitely only want to shuffle the `x_i` in question and leave all other variables intact.

title: Make it easy to convert from `count()` to `table()`
description:
In each of the infer-based DataCamp courses, there has been a lot of debate about whether to create contingency tables using base-R's `table()` or dplyr's `count()`.

`count()` is better for programming with, and fits better with the idea of doing everything in the tidyverse. So this is the natural first choice, except ...

`chisq.test()` wants to receive the results of  `table()`.

This means a tricky extra step of converting from a data frame to a table using `xtabs()`. 

To solve this, I suggest using a wrapper function around `xtabs()` to make it simple to go from one form to the other.

```r
as_table <- function(count_df, count_col = "n") {
  other_cols <- setdiff(colnames(count_df), count_col)
  spec_string <- paste(count_col, "~", paste(other_cols, collapse = " + "))
  spec <- as.formula(spec_string)
  tbl <- stats::xtabs(spec, count_df)
  attr(tbl, "call") <- NULL
  class(tbl) <- "table"
  tbl
}
```

Example usage:

```r
library(dplyr)
co2_df <- CO2 %>% count(Type, Treatment)
as_table(co2_df)
##              Treatment
##  Type          nonchilled chilled
##   Quebec              21      21
##   Mississippi         21      21
```

Here's another example that demos `count_col`, which is needed when the input is the result of calling `as.data.frame()` on a table.

```r
titanic_df <- as.data.frame(Titanic)
titanic_table <- as_table(titanic_df, count_col = "Freq")
identical(Titanic, titanic_table) # TRUE
```

title: Implement "area under the curve" in `shade_p_value()`
description:
As noted in [this](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/205#issuecomment-431433109) and [this](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/205#issuecomment-433574709) commentaries by @andrewpbray, there is a desire to illustrate p-value directly as "area under the curve". Currently function `shade_p_value()` is responsible for this, but as it is supposed to be {ggplot2}-layer-like function, it is a little bit tricky to do.

Here is a scetch of solution:

- **Compute function representing "curve"**:
    - If `method` in `visualize()` is `"theoretical"` (in `shade_p_value()` it is determined by `get_viz_method()` as is [here](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/db509aa1cc4b545be01426fe7aabffb66cde96fe/R/visualize.R#L602)) than this is a certain theoretical density.
    - If `method` is one of `"simulation"` or `"both"`:
        - *Compute histogram levels* of `visualize()` output. This should be done by building histogram plot `g` using directly [`simulation_layer()`](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/db509aa1cc4b545be01426fe7aabffb66cde96fe/R/visualize.R#L244) (this needs attaching `bins` and `...` to data, as with `get_viz_method()` solution) and extracting histogram levels with `ggplot_build(g)$data[[1]]`.
        - *Compute step function representing histogram* with `stepfun()` and data from the previous step.
- **Use `stat_function(data = data.frame(x = x_range), mapping = aes(x), fun = f, geom = "area", xlim = pval_range, fill = "pink", alpha = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE)`** where:
    - `x_range` is a range of plotted data. Depends on visualization `method` and seems to deserve computation in separate function.
    - `f` is a "curve" function from previous step.
    - `pval_range` represents borders of shaded area and depends on `obs_stat` and `direction`.

Probably better be done after implementing #212, as this is a massive visualization update.

title: Update `shade_ci()`
description:
After #229 is merged, I think it is a good idea to update `shade_ci()` to match `shade_p_value()` new behavior.

I think that actually using "area under the curve" shading during CI visualization is not a good idea. Mainly because I feel that its goal is to visualize *interval on x axis* and not something related to distribution itself. We can change current "half-plane" shading to "highlight interval on x axis" approach, but it doesn't seem to be necessary (current approach feels quite good).

So with this in mind I can only think about drawing vertical lines for CI edges starting from 0 and not from the bottom of an image (see [this comment](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/213#issuecomment-478565404)).

title: Use default+match.arg() for character arguments
description:
I regularly forget the different options for the `null` argument to `hypothesize()`. Since there is no default, I have to go and read the documentation to find out what my options are.

If the function were amended to

```r
hypothesize <- function(x, null = c("independence", "point"), ...) {
  null <- match.arg(null)
}
```

then I could just do `args(hypothesize)` to see what is available.

The same thing applies to `generate()`'s `type` argument. It's worth noting that `calculate()`'s `stat` argument is already set up this way.

title: Add the choices for point hypotheses to the fn signature
description:
Currently, it's really hard to determine what arguments can be used with point hypotheses.

There's already an open issue for improving the documentation (https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/issues/223) but I think that tweaking the function signature (in a way that shouldn't break existing code) might help.

The idea is you change the signature to this

```r
hypothesize <- function(x, null, p = NULL, mu = NULL, med = NULL, sigma = NULL) {
  
}
```

That way, it's really obvious that `p`, `mu`, `med`, and `sigma` are the only choices.

The only change to the body of `hypothesize()` is that

```r
dots <- list(...)
```

becomes

```r
dots <- list(p = p, mu = mu, med = med, sigma = sigma)
```

And in `parse_params()`, the messing about at the start with

```r
    p_ind <- grep("p", names(dots))
    mu_ind <- grep("mu", names(dots))
    med_ind <- grep("med", names(dots))
    sig_ind <- grep("sigma", names(dots))
    if (length(p_ind) + length(mu_ind) + length(med_ind) + length(sig_ind) != 
        1) {
        stop_glue("Parameter values can be only one of `p`, `mu`, `med`, or `sigma`.")
    }
```

can be simplified to

```r
  if(length(dots) != 1) {
    stop_glue("You must specify exactly one of `p`, `mu`, `med`, or `sigma`.")
  }
```

title: Use a simplified version of chisq.test()$statistic
description:
`calc_impl.Chisq()` uses `stats::chisq.test()` to retrieve the chi-squared statistic.

https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/blob/develop/R/calculate.R#L235-L239

Since you only want the statistic, not other things like the p-value, and since the input is never a matrix, you can do this more efficiently with a custom function.

```r
chisq_test_statistic <- function(x, p) {
  if (any(x < 0) || anyNA(x)) 
    stop("all entries of 'x' must be nonnegative and finite")
  n <- sum(x)
  if (n == 0) 
    stop("at least one entry of 'x' must be positive")
  E <- n * p
  sum((x - E) ^ 2 / E)
}
```

title: Change computation of two-sided p-value
description:
This issue is a result of discussion started in #203 (after [this comment](https://github.com/tidymodels/infer/pull/203#issuecomment-431078712)). I think it deserves a separate thread.

The suggestion is to change method of two-sided p-value computation in `get_p_value()` to "Chihara and Hesterberg" (CaH) approach: "For a two-sided test, we calculate both one-sided P-values, multiply the smaller by 2, and finally (if necessary) round down to 1.0 (because probabilities can never be larger than 1.0)."

There is also a desire for `get_p_value()` and `shade_p_value()` (now available only in `develop` branch) to use the same approach of computing two-sided p-value.

title: PR #262: correct observed statistic calculation in vignette
description:
Just PRed (#262) a quick correction to the calculation of the observed statistic in one of the vignettes. The observed statistic was calculated with assumed null hypothesis `mu = 0`, but later compared against a distribution generated with null hypothesis `mu = 8`. I used the `t_stat` wrapper here, but could have also used 

```
t_bar <- fli_small %>%
  specify(response = dep_delay) %>%
  calculate(stat = "t", mu = 8)
```

@mine-cetinkaya-rundel 's Issue #232 is probably relevant here. Ideally, this calculation should probably look something like:

```
t_bar <- fli_small %>%
  specify(response = dep_delay) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "point", mu = 8) %>%
  calculate(stat = "t")
```

which currently returns the original data.

Thanks to @mcconvil for calling attention to this!

The new `infer.Rmd` vignette from the `documentation` branch will have a similar example here soon.

We're currently doing 1.

title: T-test 2 levels (example)
description:
This may be addressed or intentional, but it seem as though `t_test` should not have to specify `order` in the specification, but if not (in the example from the vignette), things will fail:

# Read in the data

``` r
library(nycflights13)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(stringr)
library(infer)
set.seed(2017)
fli_small <- flights %>% 
  sample_n(size = 500) %>% 
  mutate(half_year = case_when(
    between(month, 1, 6) ~ "h1",
    between(month, 7, 12) ~ "h2"
  )) %>% 
  mutate(day_hour = case_when(
    between(hour, 1, 12) ~ "morning",
    between(hour, 13, 24) ~ "not morning"
  )) %>% 
  select(arr_delay, dep_delay, half_year, 
         day_hour, origin, carrier)
```

# Do t-test
No `order` given, but `order = NULL` in the docs, so it seems as though this should be optional:
``` r
fli_small %>% 
  t_test(formula = arr_delay ~ half_year)
#> Error in t.test.formula(formula = formula, data = ., alternative = alternative, : grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels
```

There is no missing data
``` r
fli_small %>% 
  count(half_year)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   half_year     n
#>   <chr>     <int>
#> 1 h1          255
#> 2 h2          245
```
`t.test` works just fine:
``` r
t.test(arr_delay ~ half_year, data = fli_small)
#> 
#>  Welch Two Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  arr_delay by half_year
#> t = 0.27655, df = 487.94, p-value = 0.7822
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  -5.739868  7.620333
#> sample estimates:
#> mean in group h1 mean in group h2 
#>         5.156000         4.215768
```

Can use `tidy`:
``` r
fli_small %>% 
  do(broom::tidy(t.test(.$arr_delay ~ .$half_year)))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 10
#>   estimate estimate1 estimate2 statistic p.value parameter conf.low conf.high
#>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1    0.940      5.16      4.22     0.277   0.782      488.    -5.74      7.62
#> # … with 2 more variables: method <chr>, alternative <chr>
```

title: Extend `calculate()` with `stat = "ratio of props"` and `stat = "odds ratio"`
description:
the infer randomization test is a simulation of Fisher's exact test (in the 2x2 case).  typically, Fisher's exact test is taught hand-in-hand with odds ratios. 

`infer` is a great teaching tool, and as such, it's nice to have so many different statistics to work with.  with easy connections to many statistics, students are able to see that the randomization approach is much bigger than simply the computer doing the CLT.

would be great if in the 2x2 setting, the `calculate()` function included `stat = "ratio of props"` and `stat = "odds ratio"`.

Thanks!

title: Confusion on p-value in one proportion randomisation
description:
I have a question regarding your one proportion randomisation example in the infer package, as seen here:

title: "Error: Column `stat` must be length 1" when bootstrap resampling small data sets
description:
I ran into this strange issue today. Here is a reprex:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)

the_data <- data.frame(Variable1 = c(rep("Yes", 23), rep("No", 7)), Variable2 = c( rep("F", 6), rep("M", 17), rep("M", 7)     ))

set.seed(42)

the_data %>%
  specify(Variable1 ~ Variable2, success = "Yes") %>%
  generate(reps = 229, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("F", "M"))
```

This generates the error message: 

> Error: Column `stat` must be length 1 (a summary value), not 0

Which seems to be connected to both the seed value and the number of replicates created by the bootstrap method. Changing reps = 228 resolves the issue (although it persists for several values of reps > 229). However, changing the seed to 1 allows for reps = 1000 and several smaller values. Perhaps this occurs when a particular resample contains only 1 level, rather than the expected 2?

title: bootstrap with small data set (samples not independent)
description:
Well either this is a mistake or this is how the bootstrap for difference in means should work. 
For difference in means, if the function is supposed to resample independently from the two samples then this package does not do this.  See example bellow:

Bootstrap samples only  from one of the factors: 
```
# A small data set. 
test <- mtcars %>% 
  filter(cyl ==6) %>% 
  mutate_at(vars(am), as.character) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  select(am, mpg)
```

```
set.seed(100)
 test %>% 
  specify(mpg ~am) %>% 
  generate(reps = 10, type = "bootstrap") %>% 
  group_by(replicate, am) %>% 
  summarise(out = mean(mpg)) %>% 
  summarise(out2 = out[am =="1"] - out[am=="0"])
```

Error: Column `out2` must be length 1 (a summary value), not 0

The error is the same if I use `calculate()`. 

Here we can see that `replicate` 10 only includes samples from `am==0`:

```

   specify(mpg ~am) %>%

title: Spelling of get_p_value() direction argument
description: The `direction` argument in the `get_p_value()` function takes a character string. For two-sided hypotheses this string is `"two_sided"` but since it's a character string I don't think `_` is needed. It could be a blank space or `-`.  Since we allow blank spaces in the stat argument for `calculate`, it would make sense to allow for natural spelling here too for consistency.

title: Explicit mention of "taking a random sample" in vignettes using flights data
description:
I'm reading through some of the vignettes again to make sure I'm up to date with everything, and I have a suggestion for improving the narrative, especially for those who are new to statistical inference (but might be familiar with the `nycflights13` dataset from R for Data Science or tidyverse docs (which I imagine is not an insubstantial audience for this package).

We use a random sample from `nycflights13` so we have a random sample on which we're doing inference. I think it would be nice to explicitly mention this on top of the vignettes, with something along the lines of the following: 

> "Note that the `nycflights13` data frame contains _all_ flights out of NYC airports in 2013, which is not a random sample. For the purposes of this example, we will take a random sample of 500 observations from this data frame and base our analysis on this random sample, as though we didn't have access to the full population data for 2013. This will allow us to assume independence between observations, which we couldn't with the full dataset as it is not reasonable to assume that flight delays within a day will be independent of each other." 

If there's an agreement I'm happy to do a PR. And feel free to improve the language!
